newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Low growth seen in TVB '96 net.
newsitem.headline: Low growth seen in TVB '96 net.

text.p: Growth forecasts for the 1996 earnings of Television Broadcasts Ltd (TVB) have been steadily scaled back to single digits from the high teens, but some analysts said even that may be too optimistic.
"We are expecting six percent growth to HK$513 million ($66 million) after a fairly disappointing first half," said Robert Fong, media analyst at HSBC James Capel.
There seems little chance that earnings picked up until late in 1996 at TVB, Hong Kong's largest broadcasting station, Fong said.

The company surprised analysts with a first-half downturn in earnings. For the six months ended June 30, the company reported net profit of HK$177.96 million, a 5.8 percent decline from HK$189.01 million in the year-earlier period.
The company will release its 1996 earnings report on Wednesday.
SBC Warburg has grown more cautious on the company's outlook, forecasting flat to negative growth in line with 1995's HK$485.5 million.
"There was nothing really to help their advertising rates. There just wasn't the demand for air time," said an SBC Warburg analyst.
"Even if you take into account the Olympic Games, as a whole the market was soft, so they are not able to achieve any benefits from putting up their advertising rates."
Analysts said advertising demand was soft last year because consumers were not spending freely, and retail sales reflected this trend.
"You tend to find that demand for advertising follows consumer demand in the economy," said SBC Warburg.
Government statistics show retail sales in Hong Kong rose 6.3 percent in value terms and just 1.6 percent in volume terms in 1996 compared with 1995.
In addition to weak demand for air time, TVB suffered from large cost overruns on some of its more ambitious drama series.
The company has indicated that most of those cost overruns were confined to the first half and should not hurt second-half earnings, analysts said.
TVB's operating profit margin was forecast to drop to 21.5 percent from 23 percent in 1995, said HSBC's Fong.
In years when there was active demand for air time and the company's pre-emptive bidding system for prime time slots was in full swing, margins soared.
"Just to give an example, in 1994 the company's operating profit margins rose to 34 percent," said Fong.
The mean of 31 profit estimates in The Estimate Directory released by Edinburgh Financial Services is HK$532 million, a 10 percent increase over 1995.
The company's shares close HK$0.10 lower at HK$31.70 on Monday.
